scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

The person is an 18-year-old guy with a twin sister. He's been best friends with someone named G since kindergarten. G and his sister have had a close relationship for a long time, but they finally started dating when they were 17. Everything was good for about 13 months, but then G cheated on his sister. The main character found out about the cheating and told his sister, even though G begged him not to. This led to a fight where they didn't talk for a month and a half. Eventually, G apologized, and they reconciled, even going on a ski trip together. Now, the sister is upset because the main character is still friends with G, and she's making him feel bad about it. He's trying to justify keeping the friendship because it's been 13 years, and he doesn't want to lose his best friend over this.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for him to continue the friendship with G after G cheated on his sister?

First, I need to consider the different perspectives involved here. There's the main character, his sister, and G. Each of them has their own feelings and reasons.

From the main character's perspective, he's been friends with G for a long time. They've been through a lot together, and losing that friendship would be really hard for him. He also mentions that G is genuinely sorry and that they've reconciled. He's trying to move forward and not let this incident ruin their friendship. He compares it to if his best friend cheated on someone else's partner and whether he would end the friendship, which he says he wouldn't. So, he's treating this situation the same way.

From his sister's perspective, she's hurt because her boyfriend cheated on her. She's probably feeling betrayed and emotional. She's making him feel bad for still being friends with G, which is understandable because she's going through a tough time. She might feel that by continuing the friendship, he's not supporting her or taking her feelings into account.

From G's perspective, he made a mistake by cheating. He apologized, and it seems like he's genuinely remorseful. He's trying to make amends, which is why he invited the main character on the ski trip to reconcile.

Now, considering the moral aspects. Morality often involves balancing different values and considering the well-being of others. In this case, the main character is prioritizing his long-term friendship and his own emotional well-being. On the other hand, his sister is feeling hurt and may feel that her well-being is being neglected.

I think it's important to consider the concept of forgiveness and moving forward. The main character has chosen to forgive G, which is a personal decision. However, he's also in a position where he has to consider his sister's feelings. It's a tough spot because he's caught between two people he cares about deeply.

Another angle is the idea of loyalty. The main character is loyal to his friend, but his sister might feel that he's not being loyal to her by continuing the friendship. However, loyalty doesn't necessarily mean cutting ties with someone who has wronged someone else, especially if that person has apologized and made amends.

I also think about the potential consequences of ending the friendship. The main character mentions that losing G would be unbearable, and they're planning to go to the same college together. Ending the friendship could have long-term negative effects on his life and mental health.

On the other hand, his sister is going through a tough time, and he might feel that he should support her by cutting ties with G. But it's also possible that she's not considering his feelings in this situation, expecting him to choose her over his friend without acknowledging the difficulty of that choice.

In terms of moral acceptability, I think it's a gray area. The main character is not doing anything inherently wrong by continuing the friendship. He's dealing with a difficult situation where he has to balance his own feelings, his sister's feelings, and his friendship. It's a personal choice, and while his sister might not agree, it's not necessarily morally wrong.

However, it's also important to consider whether he's being fair to his sister. By continuing the friendship, he might be making it harder for her to heal, especially if she's still upset about the cheating. But he's also an 18-year-old dealing with his own emotions and trying to navigate this situation.

In conclusion, while the main character's decision might not be the easiest or the most considerate of his sister's feelings, it's not morally wrong. He's prioritizing his own well-being and a long-standing friendship, which are valid considerations.
